statement: Two runners start together from the same point on a $400$-meter circular track and run at different constant speeds. When they run in opposite directions, they meet every $40$ seconds. When they run in the same direction, the faster runner gains a full lap on the slower one every $200$ seconds. How many seconds does the faster runner take to run one lap?

choices.misconception: I used the average of the two speeds, $5$ meters per second, and divided $400$ by it.
I solved the system correctly but answered for the slower runner, whose speed is $4$ meters per second.
I averaged the two given times, $\frac{40 + 200}{2} = 120$, instead of turning them into speeds.
I took the $200$ seconds between laps gained as the time for the faster runner to run one lap.

hints: Turn each time into a statement about speeds.

Running toward each other, together they cover $400$ meters every $40$ seconds. Running the same way, the faster one gains $400$ meters every $200$ seconds. Write one equation for the sum of the speeds and one for the difference.
With speeds $u > v$ in meters per second: $u + v = 10$ and $u - v = 2$, so $u = 6$. The faster lap takes $400 / 6$ seconds.

solutions.reliable: Let the speeds be $u > v$ meters per second. Running in opposite directions, the gap between meetings is one full lap covered by both together, so $40(u + v) = 400$ and $u + v = 10$. Running in the same direction, the faster runner gains one lap every $200$ seconds, so $200(u - v) = 400$ and $u - v = 2$. Adding, $2u = 12$, so $u = 6$ and $v = 4$. The faster runner takes $\frac{400}{6} = \frac{200}{3}$ seconds per lap. Check: $v = 4$ gives the slower runner $100$ seconds per lap, and $6 - 4 = 2$ meters per second of gain closes $400$ meters in $200$ seconds. Transferable idea: opposite directions add speeds, same direction subtracts them.
